newsitem.title: USA: Fed proposes further freedom for bank underwriting.
newsitem.headline: Fed proposes further freedom for bank underwriting.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Board voted unanimously Wednesday to issue a sweeping proposal that would further loosen restrictions on banks' activities in the securities business.
Among other things, the proposal would make it easier for bank holding companies and their securities industry affiliates to offer "one-stop shopping" to their customers.
The changes, for example, would allow a bank to issue a letter of credit to enhance the standing of a customer wishing to issue corporate bonds through the bank's securities affiliate.
Currently, customers are required to seek such letters from separate institutions.

The proposal, subject to a 60-day comment period, was the latest in a series of moves the Fed has made in recent months to ease rules governing the relationship between bank holding companies and their investment-banking affiliates.

Fed Gov. Susan Phillips said the move was part of an ongoing effort to streamline regulations and make them less burdensome. It should also help banks improve their competitiveness in the investment-banking area, she said.
Banking industry representatives, who have been pushing for such changes for quite some time, praised the move as a bold step.

"The Fed has scored a regulatory hat-trick today by proposing to lift anachronistic rules that have long outlived their usefulness," said Larry LaRocco, managing director of the ABA Securities Association, an affiliate of the American Bankers Association.
"These changes recognise how dramatically the marketplace has changed since the firewalls were adopted nine years ago," LaRocco added.

However, James Spellman, spokesman for the Securities Industry Association, cautioned against the proposal and other "piecemeal" efforts by bank regulators to "rewrite" the Depression-era Glass Steagall Act. He said such changes should be made by Congress as part of a comprehensive package.

The Glass Steagall Act generally prohibits banks from engaging in non-banking activities, although a special provision allows separately capitalised subsidiaries to conduct securities activities not permitted in banks.

In 1987, when the Fed first began allowing the existence of such subsidiaries, it subjected them to strict provisions, including a series of barriers, or "firewalls," separating the activities of the bank and the affiliate.

As part of the recent changes to those provisions, the Fed last month voted to allow the securities affiliates of banks to generate as much as a quarter of their revenue from the underwriting and dealing of securities -- an increase from the previous limit of 10 percent.
Several weeks prior to that, the Fed decided to allow employees of a bank to also work at the securities affiliate in a vote that eased three of the "firewalls."
The proposal the Fed is now considering would eliminate most of the remaining barriers and would incorporate the rest into a single statement of operating standards.
Even more dramatic changes could be in store as Congress considers dismantling the Glass Steagall Act.
Just this week, two new bills were introduced to overhaul the law.
